assumption: Long waits are caused by information or approval waits, not the queue.
risk_if_wrong: We invest in building AI-assisted information and approval workflows, whilst the real sorting bottleneck is caused by handler capacity or planning.
cheapest_test: Test the timeline of historic claim data, both simple claims and claims that take more than 4 hours to sort, using a sample of 80 claims (invented).
pass_threshold: Queue time is 15% or less of elapsed time on 4+ hour claims, so the waits come from information or approval. Elapsed time is measured from claim received to sorted; queue time is time unworked with nothing outstanding.
fail_threshold: Queue time is 30% or more of elapsed time on 4+ hour claims, so the queue is the issue and faster sorting would help the tail.
what_changes_if_wrong: If queuing is the issue and not information or approvals, look at how we can improve handler workflows. If queue time is between 15 and 30%, look at the different claim types and analyse.
notes: If there are no clear “missing information” or “waiting for approval” flags, we’ll need to pick a sample by hand.

assumption: When a claim is paid out wrongly, it’s mostly because the information that would have changed the decision was in the claim, but the handler didn’t use it.
risk_if_wrong: The wrong payouts come from missing or late data or unclear policy, so showing context to the handler doesn’t reduce wrong pay.
cheapest_test: 30 wrong payouts from reversal, recovery or complaint records, plus 30 correct records mixed in. Two experienced handlers review all 60 without knowing which is which.
pass_threshold: 30% or more of wrong payouts, with both reviewers agreeing the deciding information was in the claim when it was sorted.
fail_threshold: 10% or less of wrong payouts meet the pass bar.
what_changes_if_wrong: Fix the data at intake and clarify the policy guidance on the suspicious pile, instead of investing in building a way to show context to handlers.
notes: Between 10 and 30%: break the results down by type of information (linked claims, earlier claims, policy rules) and act only on a type that recurs. Validity check: if reviewers flag overlooked information on the 30 correct claims at half the wrong-payout rate or more, treat the result as hindsight noise.

assumption: AI-suggested sorting makes no more dangerous errors than human handlers. “Dangerous” means a wrong “simple”, the wrong payout case.
risk_if_wrong: Claims that need investigation get paid. Money goes out wrongly, the decision can’t be defended to the regulator, and handlers stop trusting the tool.
cheapest_test: Test 3 variants on 80 invented claims. Compare against labels checked by an experienced handler, and report the linked-claim subset separately. Riskiest decisions get a blind check by experienced handlers and compliance.
pass_threshold: Wrong-simple rate at or below half the handlers’ baseline wrong-simple rate, and zero errors on linked claims.
fail_threshold: Any wrong “simple” on linked claims, or a wrong-simple rate above the handlers’ baseline.
what_changes_if_wrong: The AI may only route claims toward a human (closer look or suspicious) and never clears one for payment. If it can’t meet that, stop.
notes: Depends on the label audit (L1), which is a hard requirement for this test. Between half the baseline and the baseline: investigate further.

assumption: AI-suggested sorting cuts handler time per decision without adding overrides, reclassifications or escalations.
risk_if_wrong: AI increases handler time and lengthens queues due to more escalations.
cheapest_test: Measure time to decision with and without a suggestion, plus overrides and the share sent to suspicious.
pass_threshold: 30% or more of handler time saved, with override, reclassification and escalation rates no higher than without a suggestion, across a sample of 80 invented claims.
fail_threshold: 10% or less of handler time saved, or override, reclassification or escalation rates higher than without a suggestion, across a sample of 80 invented claims.
what_changes_if_wrong: Drop AI suggestions, keep bulk sorting, and invest in improving the information and approval workflow.
notes: If assumption A1 holds, this assumption matters less because the waits come from waiting, not from deciding.

assumption: Handler labels (the pile each past claim ended in, and the 3.4% moved within 30 days) are reliable enough to use as the reference for A3a.
risk_if_wrong: A3a judges the AI against wrong answers, so it passes or fails for the wrong reason.
cheapest_test: A senior handler re-sorts 50 past claims (invented size) without seeing the original pile: 30 sampled across the three piles, and 20 that were moved within 30 days. For each moved claim, record why: new information arrived, the first pile was wrong, or a policy changed.
pass_threshold: Senior handler agrees with the final pile on 90% or more of claims.
what_changes_if_wrong: Don’t use handler labels as the reference. Use senior-handler labels for the A3a claim set instead, and treat the result as lower confidence.
notes: Runs before A3a. Between 80 and 90%: investigate which piles disagree before using the labels. Also shows what share of the 3.4% are errors rather than late information, which bears on A1.
